title: How to give feedback that changes behaviour, not just feelings
flags: VERIFICATION-LIMIT: Only the approved knowledge sheet supports the guidance. External research, organisational procedures, role permissions and causal effectiveness were not verified.
METHOD-LIMIT: A conservative writing aid, not a validated intervention or a replacement for an existing organisational method.
SCOPE-LIMIT: Ordinary colleague feedback only. Formal performance, disciplinary and safety procedures remain outside scope and unverified.
EXAMPLE-BOUNDARY: All project-update events and dialogue are hypothetical. Recipient feelings, account, agreement, feasibility and subsequent action remain unknown.
ASSESSMENT-LIMIT: Private drafts and actual workplace performance are not externally assessed.
PRESENTATION-OPEN: Light illustration is the default. Acting intensity remains unresolved. Preserve the classic explanation-led alternative with identical narration and checks.
TIMING-ADAPTATION: One stopping quiz uses a four-second question hold and a two-second answer reading hold to comply with the script-stage pause rule and gate. Other questions do not stop playback.

SCREEN-CONTRACT: Current anchors are the only newly legible words. Previously voiced prose becomes unlettered lines outside its inspection moment. Quiz metadata retains the full supplied options; the screen magnifies the same draft's action-and-occasion excerpts.

presentation_options.default: Lightly illustrated story-cartoon, with the same two neutral peer colleagues, shared-update message, planning note and feedback draft. Document editing carries the progression. No recipient acting or successful outcome.
presentation_options.classic_alternative: Explanation-led document compositions with the same objects, wording, annotations, practice and payoff. Omit characters. Neither treatment is claimed superior.

persona_audit.method: Manual review of full-stop sentence groups and interrogatives, including quoted requests. Commas are breath boundaries. Questions use interrogative delivery rather than question-mark phrase endings.
persona_audit.rhythm_check: Long multi-phrase sentences alternate with short landings. Every beat lands below eight words. Sentence-length spread exceeds the persona minimum. No three consecutive sentences have equal lengths.

narration: Imagine a colleague sends a project update,
without noting that the delivery date has changed.
You plan using the old date.
beats.visual_intent: Presenter intro beside an illustrated workplace inset. The update has a delivery-date gap; the giver's planning note uses old date. Neutral peer colleagues, no numerical dates or reply.

grounding.claim: The hypothetical update omits a changed delivery date.
The giver hypothetically plans using the old date.

beats.delivery: Warm. Make Imagine unmistakable.

narration: You are about to write,
Please be more considerate,
but what should change in the next update.
Name the action.
beats.visual_intent: Close on the same giver's unsent draft. The broad request sits beside the update and an empty future-action slot. No recipient reaction.

grounding.claim: The hypothetical broad request does not specify the next-update action.
Identify the desired future action.

beats.delivery: Ask the first three phrases as one question. Brief natural pause, no stopping hold.

narration: We will revise that message together,
then use the same check on your feedback.
The destination is a clearer request.
beats.visual_intent: The presenter indicates the existing draft and a second empty sheet for the viewer. Keep the workplace inset; do not display an agenda.

grounding.claim: The writing destination is an identifiable requested action and occasion.

beats.delivery: Promise a clearer draft, not recipient change.

narration: Think of a conversation where you wanted change,
what reaction did you notice,
and what action did you want next.
Keep the details private.
beats.visual_intent: Two separate empty annotation spaces sit beside the recurring draft: reaction and action. Neither receives an invented feeling or a viewer incident.

grounding.claim: Identify the future action separately from the emotional reaction.
Reaction alone does not establish behaviour change.

beats.delivery: First three phrases form a question. Do not stop playback.

narration: Here is the tricky part.
A reaction to feedback does not establish,
that workplace behaviour has changed.
Keep those separate.
beats.visual_intent: Hold the two empty spaces beside the message. Reaction belongs beside the conversation; workplace behaviour belongs beside the future-action space. No causal arrow.

grounding.claim: An emotional reaction alone is not evidence of changed workplace behaviour.

beats.misconception: An emotional reaction proves workplace behaviour changed.
beats.delivery: Warning first. Slow on does not establish.

narration: How you deliver feedback can affect,
whether someone is willing to discuss it,
but does respectful wording ensure they are receptive.
No, context still matters.
beats.visual_intent: Attach a discuss tab to the draft. Leave the recipient reply area empty. Context is an open margin annotation, not an invented diagnosis.

grounding.claim: Delivery can affect willingness to discuss feedback.
Respectful wording cannot ensure receptiveness; person, relationship and context matter.

beats.delivery: First three phrases form a question. Answer gently; feelings are not a failure.

narration: Back at the update, the next action matters,
separately from the colleague's reaction to this conversation.
Name what should change next.
beats.visual_intent: Return to the update and planning note. The future-action slot remains separate from the empty reaction space. Hold this composition for the pocket rule.

grounding.claim: Plan around the desired future action.
Reaction alone does not establish changed behaviour.

beats.delivery: Brisk pocket rule.

narration: Your draft still says, please be more considerate,
but does that name an action for next time.
Not yet, we can make it explicit.
beats.visual_intent: Inspect the same unsent draft and its empty action slot. Keep the broad request attached to the message, without blame symbols or a recipient expression.

grounding.claim: The broad hypothetical wording does not identify a next action.
The supplied revision makes its requested action explicit.

beats.delivery: Ask the first two phrases as a question, then answer.

narration: In the last project update,
the changed delivery date was not noted.
It identifies an omission, not character.
beats.visual_intent: Replace the broad-request draft area with the supplied situation-and-omission clause. Align its omission span with the original update's gap. This is an actual draft revision.

grounding.claim: The hypothetical revision identifies the situation and omitted changed date.
Describe the specific omission rather than character.
Identify the situation where the omission occurred.

beats.delivery: Read the first two phrases as proposed wording, then explain.

narration: Here is the tricky part.
Could you substantiate this example,
without assuming your interpretation must be correct.
Specific does not mean certain.
beats.visual_intent: The original update lies beside the revised draft. Substantiate attaches to the original message; interpretation attaches to the feedback. Keep those objects distinct.

grounding.claim: Use an example that can be substantiated.
Specific description does not make an interpretation automatically correct.

beats.delivery: Warning first. Ask the middle two phrases as a question.

narration: I used the old date,
to plan my work.
Explain why it mattered at work.
That consequence does not establish motive.
beats.visual_intent: Add the consequence line beneath the grounded account. Connect it to the same planning note, never to a thought bubble on the colleague.

grounding.claim: Old-date planning is the example's stipulated consequence.
The supplied revision includes this consequence wording.
Explain a work consequence without asserting an inferred motive.

beats.delivery: Read the first two phrases as draft wording. Separate consequence from motive.

narration: With an uncertain consequence, what can you establish,
rather than presenting a possibility as an established result.
Describe a concern or possibility.
beats.visual_intent: A margin annotation beside the consequence line offers concern or possibility. The running example's stipulated planning note remains unchanged; this is a writing caution.

grounding.claim: An uncertain consequence should be labelled a concern or possibility, not an established result.

beats.delivery: Ask the first two phrases as one question. Slow on uncertain.

narration: For the next update,
could you flag any changed delivery date,
in the message.
Write a recognisable request.
beats.visual_intent: Add the supplied peer request below the consequence. Put short action spans and the occasion beside their respective marking tools. The recipient does not act.

grounding.claim: The supplied request asks for flagging changed delivery dates in the next update.
Request an action the colleague can recognise and attempt.
Give the next action a clear occasion.
Frame ordinary peer feedback as a request.

beats.delivery: Read the first three phrases with polite question intonation. Slow on flag and next update.

narration: Where is the action, and when does it apply,
if the request is flagging a changed delivery date.
The occasion is the next update.
beats.visual_intent: Hold the request area large. Keep action and occasion markers directly attached to their spans. The reply space remains empty while the viewer locates them.

grounding.claim: The revision requests flagging a changed delivery date in the next update.
Check whether the action and occasion are identifiable.

beats.delivery: First two phrases form a question. Natural thinking space, no stopping hold.

narration: Would that work for you,
or is there a constraint we should account for.
Invite their account before settling the solution.
beats.visual_intent: Place a separate discussion strip below the prepared request. Its prompt spans face an empty recipient reply area. It is not an agreement seal.

grounding.claim: This is the supplied hypothetical discussion prompt.
Invite the colleague's account before treating the solution as settled.

beats.delivery: First two phrases are the discussion question. Do not supply a reply.

narration: Choose the change, then ground your account,
make a request and invite discussion,
then discuss the next action.
Keep your existing method, too.
beats.visual_intent: The same draft becomes a compact writing aid: intention margin, grounded account, request strip, discussion strip and next-action marker. Signal each in spoken order, without numbered steps.

grounding.claim: Choose the desired future change.
Ground the account in situation and specific action.
Make a recognisable request.
Invite discussion before settlement.
Discuss a next action and occasion.
This clarity criterion is not a validated measure of effectiveness or a universal replacement method.

beats.delivery: Name the sequence only now. Keep existing method is permission, not a comparative effectiveness claim.

narration: The request has gone from our draft,
what was the action, and what was the occasion.
Recall them before rereading the wording.
beats.visual_intent: The same feedback draft has its request strip hidden, leaving an obvious blank below the grounded account and consequence. Keep the original message and planning note.

grounding.claim: Recall the example's flagging action and next-update occasion.
Action and occasion are the clarity criterion.

beats.delivery: First two phrases form a callback question. Continue without a stopping hold.

narration: But what should the colleague do next,
and where does that belong in the message.
The future request is missing.
beats.visual_intent: Inspect the blank request strip below the remaining past-problem lines. Do not fill it yet. The empty space itself identifies the missing writing job.

grounding.claim: The situation and consequence alone omit the revision's requested future action.
The next action and occasion should be explicit.

beats.delivery: Ask the first two phrases as a question, then identify the gap.

narration: Use the anchors, changed delivery date and next update,
to compose your own request while we keep going.
Exact wording is not required.
beats.visual_intent: Attach only the two content anchors to the blank strip. Keep the completed model hidden, giving the viewer room to formulate wording without another incident.

grounding.claim: The example's request concerns a changed delivery date in the next update.
The criterion concerns identifiable action and occasion, not exact phrasing.

beats.delivery: Continue naturally. This is faded practice, not another pause.

narration: For the next update,
could you flag any changed delivery date,
in the message.
Compare the action and occasion.
beats.visual_intent: Restore the original request in the same strip. Mark action and occasion beside their spans, so the viewer compares the content of their wording rather than memorising a sentence.

grounding.claim: This is the supplied hypothetical request.
Compare requested action and occasion using the clarity criterion.

beats.delivery: First three phrases are the request question. No correctness judgement of unseen viewer wording.

narration: Can they identify the requested action,
and when it applies, from your wording alone.
That is our clarity check.
beats.visual_intent: The two markers now form a compact inspection tool attached to the restored request. Name the clarity check only after the viewer has used it.

grounding.claim: The clarity check asks whether action and occasion can be identified from the wording.

beats.delivery: Ask the first two phrases as one question. Slightly slower when naming the check.

narration: Beside that request, keep the invitation to discuss,
because clearer wording does not settle their account,
or establish that they have agreed.
Describe, request, then discuss.
beats.visual_intent: Hold the request strip beside the separate discussion strip and empty reply space. Do not merge the request with an agreement marker. Settle on the existing draft.

grounding.claim: Invite the colleague's account before treating a solution as settled.
A request is not agreement until the recipient agrees.

beats.delivery: Steady consolidation, then the pocket rule.

narration: Two drafts of the same message are ready,
which one names what to do and when.
Judge the wording, not the reaction.
beats.visual_intent: Two versions of the recurring message lie on the same desk. Equal styling and no answer markings. Introduce the judgement criterion before the stopping quiz.

grounding.claim: Judge identifiable action and occasion in the wording.
Reaction alone does not establish behaviour change.

beats.delivery: Ask the first two phrases as one question. Do not reveal the quiz answer.

narration: Here is the tricky part.
Your request may not fit their circumstances.
A request is not an agreement.
beats.visual_intent: Beside the two drafts, keep a blank reply area and an unresolved circumstances annotation. No acceptance tick or completed future update.

grounding.claim: A clear request can be infeasible or inappropriate in the colleague's circumstances.
A request does not establish agreement.

beats.misconception: Clear respectful wording means the colleague will agree and change.
beats.delivery: Warning first, then separate fit from agreement.

narration: Could resources, authority or skills limit the requested action,
when we do not yet know which constraint applies.
Ask, rather than diagnose.
beats.visual_intent: Attach resources, authority and skills as question tabs to the unresolved circumstances margin, in spoken order. None is selected as the colleague's actual constraint.

grounding.claim: Resources, authority or skills can limit action.
Do not assume which constraint applies without exploring it.

beats.delivery: Ask the first two phrases as one question. No diagnostic tone.

narration: Which draft names an action and occasion,
A, flag a changed delivery date next update,
or B, please be more considerate.
Pause the video and decide.
beats.visual_intent: Show two equal draft objects. A exposes its action and occasion extracts; its earlier descriptive prose is unlettered lines. B displays the broad request. No highlight, tick or answer cue.

grounding.claim: A represents the supplied hypothetical revision.
B is the supplied hypothetical broad wording.
The judgement criterion is identifiable action and occasion.

recall.question: Which draft lets the colleague identify what is requested and when it applies?

options.wording: In the last project update, the changed delivery date was not noted. I used the old date to plan my work. For the next update, could you flag any changed delivery date in the message?

beats.delivery: Now the stopping check. First three phrases form one question. End exactly with pause the video and decide, then remain silent for the hold.

narration: A requests flagging any changed delivery date,
in the next update, while B,
asks for consideration without specifying the next action.
That is the difference.
beats.visual_intent: Only after the hold, mark A's action and occasion. Beside B, show consideration facing an empty next-action slot. The picture explains the tempting quality-versus-action confusion.

grounding.claim: A specifies flagging a changed delivery date in the next update.
B expresses consideration without specifying what to do next.
A meets the action-and-occasion criterion more clearly.

recall.why: It specifies flagging a changed delivery date and the next-update occasion.
recall.tempting_wrong: B expresses a desired quality but leaves the next action unspecified.

beats.delivery: Answer directly. Explain only the listed tempting option. The final silent hold is reading time for this answer, not another stopping question.

narration: Does that establish agreement or the next update's contents.
No, neither agreement nor follow-through is established.
beats.visual_intent: Keep the stronger draft's markers, with the recipient reply and future update represented by empty spaces. The writing problem is solved; neither space becomes an outcome.

grounding.claim: The revision does not establish agreement or subsequent behaviour.

beats.delivery: Ask the first sentence. Answer without suggesting likely feelings or success.

narration: Would that work for you,
or is there a constraint we should account for.
Feedback cannot guarantee agreement or change.
beats.visual_intent: Bring back the separate discussion strip below the judged draft. Keep the reply area empty. Settle the section on a clear request with an unresolved conversation.

grounding.claim: This hypothetical prompt invites discussion without supplying a response.
Discussion need not produce agreement.
Feedback alone cannot guarantee behaviour change.

beats.delivery: First two phrases are the supplied question. Calm limit, not a discouraging verdict.

narration: Choose ordinary feedback you are preparing for a colleague,
and keep the details private.
Now you.
beats.visual_intent: Replace the completed model's inspection area with an empty private draft sheet on the same desk. No invented viewer incident fills it. Keep only short drafting prompts.

grounding.claim: The transfer task concerns ordinary colleague feedback framed as a request.

beats.delivery: Invite, do not demand disclosure. No new stopping pause.

narration: If no suitable situation comes to mind,
rewrite our hypothetical project update independently,
without copying our complete draft.
Keep it labelled hypothetical.
beats.visual_intent: The empty draft has a small project-update reference object beside it as the fallback. The complete model remains hidden, so this is independent drafting.

grounding.claim: The fallback uses the existing invented project-update situation.
The independent revision uses action-and-occasion clarity rather than exact copying.

beats.delivery: Make the fallback optional. Continue without a hold.

narration: On your draft, in that future situation,
what do you want the colleague to do differently.
Write that intention first.
beats.visual_intent: Attach a future-situation prompt to the blank draft's margin. Leave the response space empty. The learner supplies their own intended change privately.

grounding.claim: Identify what the colleague should do differently in a relevant future situation.

beats.delivery: First two phrases form a question. No stopping hold.

narration: Next, locate an example you can substantiate,
including the situation and the specific action or omission.
Replace any broad character judgement.
beats.visual_intent: The blank sheet gains an evidence margin and a grounded-account area. Situation and action-or-omission prompts sit together. Do not invent an observation for the viewer.

grounding.claim: Use a substantiable example and identify its situation.
Describe a specific action or omission rather than character.

beats.delivery: Practical drafting instruction, not a list to memorise.

narration: Add the relevant work consequence,
without claiming a motive behind the action.
If uncertain, describe a concern or possibility.
Keep your account grounded.
beats.visual_intent: A blank consequence area sits beneath the grounded account. Its margin offers concern or possibility for uncertainty. The colleague's motive remains unrepresented.

grounding.claim: Explain the work consequence without presenting inferred motive as fact.
Label uncertain consequences as concerns or possibilities.

beats.delivery: Slow briefly on If uncertain, then return to drafting pace.

narration: Request an action they can recognise and attempt,
and name its occasion.
For peers, make it a request.
beats.visual_intent: Attach the established action and occasion marking tools to the viewer's empty request area. No managerial badge or command icon appears.

grounding.claim: Request a recognisable, attemptable action.
Name a clear occasion for the next action.
Frame ordinary peer feedback as a request.

beats.delivery: Warm, direct peer framing.

narration: What might their account add to your understanding,
before you treat your proposed solution as settled.
Discuss whether the action is feasible.
beats.visual_intent: Add a separate discussion area beside the blank request. The colleague's account is an empty space, not a predicted explanation. Keep feasibility open.

grounding.claim: Invite the colleague's account before treating the solution as settled.
A clear request can still be infeasible in the colleague's circumstances.

beats.delivery: Ask the first two phrases as one question. Respect their perspective.

narration: Underline the requested action in your draft,
then underline the occasion when it should happen.
If either is missing, revise that part.
beats.visual_intent: The two marking tools rest beside blank underlining targets on the private draft. Do not display a completed model or pretend the viewer has passed.

grounding.claim: Check whether requested action and occasion are identifiable in the wording.

beats.delivery: Concrete self-review. No pause instruction.

narration: A follow-up after the relevant occasion can check,
whether the intended action occurred, but would that,
prove your feedback caused it.
No, not by itself.
beats.visual_intent: Place a follow-up note beside the draft, separate from the proposed conversation. Its action-occurrence space remains blank. Do not draw a successful future update or causal arrow.

grounding.claim: Follow-up can check whether the intended action occurred.
Observed follow-through does not by itself establish feedback caused it.

beats.delivery: First three phrases form a question. Emphasise the difference between occurrence and cause.

narration: Use this for ordinary colleague feedback,
without assuming it establishes your authority,
or verifies your organisation's procedures.
Finish your draft privately after viewing.
beats.visual_intent: Hold the private draft with open role-and-procedure margin questions. No invented policy document or authority stamp. Keep the model hidden while drafting can continue later.

grounding.claim: Ordinary peer feedback should not presume managerial authority.
This sheet does not establish authority or organisational procedures.

beats.delivery: Clear scope boundary. Finishing later is permission, not another stopping task.

narration: Beside your own draft, recall the clarity check,
what action, and on what occasion.
Keep both identifiable.
beats.visual_intent: Bring the opening update back beside the viewer's blank draft. Keep only the familiar two marking tools. This is a quiet callback, not a new test.

grounding.claim: Recall the criterion of identifiable action and occasion.

beats.delivery: First two phrases form a question. Warm, non-stopping recall.

narration: We named the last project update and the omission,
then explained planning with the old date.
What does the revised draft request.
beats.visual_intent: Return to the same update, planning note and prepared revision. Their spatial alignment recalls the writing work without replaying construction. Hold the request area for the next beat.

grounding.claim: The revision names the last update, omission and old-date planning consequence.

beats.delivery: Ask the last sentence as the opening situation's question. Answer immediately in the next beat.

narration: Flag any changed delivery date in the message,
for the next project update.
The request is explicit, their response unknown.
beats.visual_intent: Hold the revised request with only its action and occasion marked. The separate discussion strip remains represented by unlettered lines; the recipient reply and later outcome remain empty.

grounding.claim: The requested action is flagging changed delivery dates in the next update.
Explicit wording does not establish agreement, feasibility or subsequent behaviour.

beats.delivery: Answer the hook. Do not imply a completed conversation.

narration: On your draft, mark the action and occasion,
keep unresolved context questions for the conversation.
Follow-up checks action, not what caused it.
beats.visual_intent: Presenter outro beside the private draft and the recurring project-update inset. Keep the two markers and open context margin. A blank follow-up note remains separate.

grounding.claim: Review action and occasion clarity.
Invite context before settlement.
Follow-up can check action, not establish feedback causation.

beats.delivery: Quiet final review, without a new quiz or pause.

narration: Return to that colleague with a clearer request,
not a promise about how they will respond.
Make it clear, discuss it, then check.
beats.visual_intent: The presenter closes beside the opening desk, now with the prepared draft and compact marking tools. End before any recipient reply or future update. Preserve the same stable classic composition as an alternative.

grounding.claim: Make the requested action and occasion clear.
Invite discussion rather than treating the solution as settled.
Feedback cannot guarantee behaviour change.
Follow-up can check whether action occurred.

beats.delivery: Warm pocket rule. Finish decisively, without a success scene.
